title: What are default and static methods in interfaces, and why were default methods added for backward compatibility (e.g. `forEach` on Collections)?
shortTitle: What are default and static methods in interfaces?

s1_definition.profdef: Before Java 8, interfaces could ONLY have abstract methods (no body). This meant adding a new method to an existing interface broke ALL implementing classes. Java 8 introduced `default` methods (methods with a body in an interface — implementing classes inherit them without overriding) and `static` methods (utility methods tied to the interface, called via `InterfaceName.method()`). The primary motivation was BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: the Java team needed to add `forEach()`, `stream()`, `removeIf()`, `sort()` to `Iterable`, `Collection`, and `List` — but millions of existing implementations would break. Default methods let them add these without modifying a single implementing class. `default void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action)` was added to `Iterable` — every `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashSet` got it FOR FREE.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the RBI (Reserve Bank) mandates that all banks must add "UPI transfer" as a service. Before Java 8, every bank (implementing class) had to write the UPI logic individually — 100 banks, 100 implementations, some might miss it. With default methods, RBI provides a DEFAULT UPI implementation in the banking interface itself. Banks get it automatically. If HDFC wants a custom implementation, it can override. If SBI is fine with the default, it does nothing. Zero breaking changes.
s1_definition.oneliner: Default method = body in interface, inherited by all impls, enables backward-compatible evolution. Static method = utility on interface, called via InterfaceName.method(), NOT inherited.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Before Java 8, interfaces could ONLY have abstract methods (no body). This meant adding a new method to an existing interface broke ALL implementing classes. Java 8 introduced `default` methods (methods with a body in an interface — implementing classes inherit them without overriding) and `static` methods (utility methods tied to the interface, called via `InterfaceName.method()`). The primary motivation was BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: the Java team needed to add `forEach()`, `stream()`, `removeIf()`, `sort()` to `Iterable`, `Collection`, and `List` — but millions of existing implementations would break. Default methods let them add these without modifying a single implementing class. `default void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action)` was added to `Iterable` — every `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashSet` got it FOR FREE.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the RBI (Reserve Bank) mandates that all banks must add "UPI transfer" as a service. Before Java 8, every bank (implementing class) had to write the UPI logic individually — 100 banks, 100 implementations, some might miss it. With default methods, RBI provides a DEFAULT UPI implementation in the banking interface itself. Banks get it automatically. If HDFC wants a custom implementation, it can override. If SBI is fine with the default, it does nothing. Zero breaking changes.

**One line to remember:** Default method = body in interface, inherited by all impls, enables backward-compatible evolution. Static method = utility on interface, called via InterfaceName.method(), NOT inherited.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's legacy `AccountService` interface has been in production for 5 years with 12 implementing classes (SavingsAccountService, CurrentAccountService, NRIAccountService, etc.).** The product team wants to add three new features: formatted balance display, transaction summary, and balance alerts. Adding abstract methods would require modifying all 12 classes. The team uses default methods to add features without touching any existing class.

**What the project will show:** Legacy interface evolving with default methods, static factory methods on the interface, existing implementations automatically inheriting new functionality, optional override for custom behavior, and the `forEach`/`stream` backward-compatibility pattern.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Request: GET /savings/SAV2001/summary. Spring resolves `@Qualifier("savingsService")` → SavingsAccountService.

**Step 2.** `savingsService.getSummary("SAV2001")` is called. SavingsAccountService does NOT override `getSummary()` — the DEFAULT method from AccountService interface runs.

**Step 3.** Default `getSummary()` calls `getAccount("SAV2001")` — this IS overridden by SavingsAccountService → loads from DB via JPA.

**Step 4.** Default `getSummary()` calls `getFormattedBalance("SAV2001")` — SavingsAccountService does NOT override this → DEFAULT runs → formats as "₹1,25,000.50".

**Step 5.** Default `getSummary()` calls `getBalanceAlert("SAV2001")` — DEFAULT runs → 125000 > 5000 → "(Recommended) Balance healthy".

**Step 6.** Now same request but for CurrentAccountService: `getSummary()` is still default, BUT `getFormattedBalance()` IS overridden → returns "Business Balance: ₹850000.00 (OD Limit available)". The default `getSummary()` calls the OVERRIDDEN version via polymorphism.
sections.s5c_hld:
**What is HLD?** The platform-wide view. Here default methods let the bank add new behavior to an existing interface (used by dozens of implementations) WITHOUT breaking any of them — HLD shows the shared interface evolving safely across many services.

```
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    HLD — Evolving a Shared Interface via Default Methods (no breakage)
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Payments svc│  │ Loans svc    │  │ Cards svc    │  ← Client services
  │ impl Ledger │  │ impl Ledger  │  │ impl Ledger  │   (all share one API)
  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
         └────────────────┼─────────────────┘ in-process / library
                          ▼
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Shared library: Ledger interface         │  ← Application Layer
         │  + post(entry)              (abstract)     │
         │  + default reverse(id)      (NEW, v2)      │  added, old impls OK
         │  + static emptyBatch()      (helper)       │
         └──────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                JDBC │
                     ▼
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ PostgreSQL       │  ← ledger_entries
         └──────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Observability: Prometheus, ELK, Jaeger           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The HLD insight: the Ledger interface is implemented by Payments, Loans, and Cards services. Before Java 8, adding a new `reverse()` method would break all three. With a default method, the new behavior ships with a ready body, so old implementations keep compiling and running — this is exactly why Collection got default `forEach`, `stream`, and `removeIf` without breaking the entire ecosystem.
sections.s5d_lld:
**What is LLD?** Zoom into the interface and its implementations to show how a default method provides a body that all implementors inherit for free, while static methods provide shared helpers.

```
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       LLD — Default & Static Methods for Backward Compatibility
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Template Method (via default): default reverse() calls post()    │
  │     WHY: common algorithm in interface, specifics in impl         │
  │  Static Factory (on interface): Ledger.emptyBatch()               │
  │     WHY: shared helper co-located with the type                   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  O: add default method = extend interface, NO change to impls      │
  │  L: every Ledger impl honors the inherited default behavior        │
  │  I: Collection's forEach/stream kept the interface usable, small   │
  │  D: services depend on the Ledger interface, not concrete classes  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           <<interface>> Ledger             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────│
  │  + post(entry: Entry): void       abstract │  impl MUST provide
  │  + default reverse(id): void      INHERITED │  body ships here
  │  + default forEach(action): void  INHERITED │  (like Collection)
  │  + static emptyBatch(): List<Entry>         │  NOT inherited
  └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
      ┌───────────┼────────────────┐ implements (inherit defaults free)
      ▼           ▼                ▼
  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
  │ SqlLedger│ │ FileLedger│ │ MockLedger   │
  │+post()   │ │+post()   │ │+post()       │
  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────────┘
    (none had to change when reverse() default was added)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. PaymentsService uses SqlLedger (written before reverse existed)
  2.   → ledger.reverse("ENT-100")        inherited default runs
  3.     → this.post(reversingEntry)       calls impl's own post()
  4.       (Rajesh SAV2001 debit of Rs.50,000 reversed as credit)
  5.   → List<Entry> batch = Ledger.emptyBatch()   static helper
  6.   → accounts.forEach(a -> log(a))     Collection default forEach
```

The LLD shows the mechanism: `reverse()` is a default method, so it carries a body (`this.post(...)`) that every implementor inherits without writing a line — old `SqlLedger`, `FileLedger`, and `MockLedger` keep working. Static `emptyBatch()` is a shared helper on the interface. This is precisely how `Collection.forEach` was added in Java 8 as a default method so lambdas could iterate any collection without breaking existing implementations.
sections.s6_takeaway:
Default methods were added in Java 8 primarily for backward compatibility. The Java team needed to add methods like forEach, stream, and removeIf to existing interfaces like Iterable and Collection, but adding abstract methods would break millions of implementing classes worldwide. Default methods solve this by providing a method body directly in the interface — implementing classes inherit the behavior automatically without any code change. ArrayList got forEach, stream, and sort without modifying its source code. This is the interface evolution pattern: add new functionality to existing interfaces without breaking binary compatibility.

In my account evolution service, the AccountService interface has one original abstract method (getAccount) and three default methods added later (getFormattedBalance, getBalanceAlert, getSummary). SavingsAccountService only implements getAccount and gets all three defaults for free. CurrentAccountService overrides getFormattedBalance with a custom "Business Balance" format but inherits the other two defaults. The key insight is that the default getSummary method calls getFormattedBalance — when called on CurrentAccountService, it dispatches to the overridden version via polymorphism, showing that defaults work with the standard method dispatch mechanism.

Static methods on interfaces are utility methods that belong to the interface namespace, called via `InterfaceName.method()`. Unlike default methods, they are NOT inherited by implementing classes and cannot be overridden. They replace the old pattern of companion utility classes like `Collections.sort()` — in Java 8, `Comparator.comparing()` and `Predicate.not()` are static methods on the interface itself. In my example, `AccountService.calculateInterest()` is a static utility that any class can call without implementing the interface.

keyPoints: Default: method with body in interface — backward-compatible evolution
Static: utility method on interface — called via InterfaceName.method()
Default added in Java 8 to evolve Collection API without breaking implementations
Static NOT inherited — must call on the declaring interface
